'''''Pereskia grandifolia''''' ('''rose cactus'''; [[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] '''''Rhodocactus grandifolius''''') is a [[species]] of [[cactus]] native to eastern and southern [[Brazil]]. Like all species in the genus ''[[Pereskia]]'' and unlike most cacti, it has persistent leaves. It was first described in 1819. It is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] and has naturalized outside its native range.

==Description==
Although ''Pereskia grandifolia'' is a cactus by classification, it takes the form of a [[shrub]] or small [[tree]], {{cvt|2|-|5|m|ft|0}} in height, exceptionally {{cvt|10|m|ft|0}}. Young twigs are green or reddish with conspicuous white spots marking the [[stoma]]ta. Its trunk has grayish-brown bark and has a diameter of up to {{cvt|20|cm|in|0}}. The [[areole]]s are rounded, cushion-shaped, and with grayish or brownish [[Trichome#Plant trichomes|tomentum]]. On the twigs, they are {{cvt|3|-|7|mm|in|1}} across and up to {{cvt|12|mm|in|1}} on the main trunk. The areoles can have one to three or occasionally four leaves (brachyblast leaves) in addition to spines. The spines range from black to brown, the number at each areole gradually increasing with age; new twigs can have spineless areoles, while the trunk areoles may have up to 90 spines, each {{cvt|2|-|6.5|cm|in|1}} long. The leaves vary in size, and are usually from {{cvt|9|-|6.5|cm|in|1}} long, but can be shorter or up to {{cvt|30|cm|in|1}} long. They are entire, with shapes ranging from elliptic to ovate and obovate-lanceolate. The dense [[inflorescence]] develops at the ends of stems and also laterally from the areoles of upper parts of the main shoots and twigs. It usually has 10-15 flowers, but sometimes has 30 or more. The flowers which may be pale pink through to purplish-pink are showy and rose-like, about {{cvt|3|–|5|cm|in|1}} across. The fruit is very variable in size and shape, and is green, yellowish or reddish-green when ripe. It contains many glossy black seeds.<ref name=Leue86/>

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described by [[Adrian Hardy Haworth]] in 1819. It was transferred to ''Rhodocactus'' as ''R. grandifolius'' by [[Frederik Marcus Knuth (taxonomist)|Frederik Marcus Knuth]] in 1936.<ref name=IPNI_219420-2/> However, this was not accepted by most botanists, and ''Rhodocactus'' was sunk into a broadly [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscribed]] ''Pereskia''. [[Molecular phylogenetics|Molecular phylogenetic]] studies from 2005 onwards suggested that with this circumscription, ''Pereskia'' was not [[Monophyly|monophyletic]], and consisted of three clades.<ref name=EdwaNyffDono05/><ref name=BarcYessHawk11/><ref name=AsaiMiya16/> In 2016, the genus ''Rhodocactus'' was revived for one of these clades, which included ''R. grandifolius''.<ref name=AsaiMiya16/> {{As of|2026|April}} the transfer was not accepted by [[Plants of the World Online]].<ref name=POWO_282498-2/>

==Distribution==
The species is native to eastern and southern [[Brazil]]. It is widely cultivated in other parts of South America, the [[West Indies]] and beyond, and has become naturalized in some of these countries, including [[Vietnam]].<ref name=POWO_282498-2/>

==Uses==
''Pereskia grandifolia'' is grown as an [[ornamental plant]], appreciated for its flowers. It is also used as a hedge.<ref name=Leue86/> Its leaves can be eaten as a salad or used in stews.<ref name=Reye98/>
